session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — what they eat, where they spend time, who they spend it with — rather than as subjects of a study about gender or food politics. The collective identity is 'men talking about their own habits and experiences', not 'men being studied for their attitudes to masculinity'. This keeps the framing grounded and behavioural from the outset, reducing the pull toward socially curated answers.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): highest risk of socially desirable or performatively self-aware responses — men may either defensively deny gender influence or over-claim it to seem progressive. Requires careful behavioural grounding and patience with surface-level answers before probing deeper.

Plant-based eating as a lived possibility (Section 4): framing this as a real personal scenario rather than an abstract policy opinion will be critical. Participants may deflect into logistics or cost without revealing underlying identity or social barriers. Push for specific social and relational obstacles.

Social dynamics within the group: three men of similar age and life stage may converge quickly on shared norms. Consensus risk is a standing concern — especially around meat-eating as 'natural', cost as a barrier, and gender-as-irrelevant as a default answer.

What would actually make plant-based foods more appealing (Section 5): risk of generic marketing-speak answers ('better taste', 'lower price'). Need to push toward concrete personal scenarios and social contexts where they could actually imagine making different choices.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Urban North West participant — may bring a more cosmopolitan or diverse food-scene framing. Age 53 suggests established habits and possibly stronger views on what counts as a 'proper' meal. Watch for whether he anchors discussion in practical or identity terms.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: None at outset — monitor for dominance if he is the most fluent speaker early on.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Suburban South East — may reflect more aspirational or health-conscious food norms typical of that demographic context. Age 50, possible family-meal framing. Could be the voice most likely to give socially acceptable progressive answers worth probing beneath.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Watch for polished self-presentation — probe for behaviour, not stated values.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Rural/village East of England — may have the most practically grounded and traditionally framed food habits. Age 52, possibly more resistant to plant-based framing on practical or cultural grounds. Could be the natural source of counter-consensus views, or alternatively the most reticent.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: If he goes quiet in Sections 3–5, prioritise a warm reactivation — his perspective is likely the most differentiated from urban norms.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability: all three men may moderate their stated views on masculinity and food in front of each other, especially if they sense the study is 'about' gender. Behavioural grounding (asking about specific moments, real past events) is the main mitigation.

Consensus convergence: similar age and life stage increases risk of rapid agreement on shared norms (e.g. meat as normal, plant-based as niche or feminine, cost as the main barrier). Plan sharpening moves and invite-dissent interventions if the group starts echoing each other.

Abstract moralising: the topic touches on environment, health, and gender politics — participants may drift into abstract opinions rather than personal behaviour. Keep pulling toward concrete experiences.
Time pressure: only three participants and six sections in 45 minutes. Sections 3, 4, and 5 carry the research weight — do not let Sections 1 and 2 run long, even if conversation is lively.

Plant-based framing: the term 'plant-based' may carry brand-awareness baggage (Beyond Meat, Oatly, etc.) that narrows responses. Stay alert to whether participants are talking about highly processed substitutes vs. vegetables, pulses, and traditional plant foods — these may have very different gendered meanings.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): hold back. Light touch. Let participants introduce themselves and warm up. Probe only if something unexpectedly rich appears — do not exhaust early topics. Section 3 (gender and food): moderate directivity. Let the question land, observe initial answers, then probe specifically for behaviour over attitude. If answers are abstract or dismissive, use behavioural grounding. If answers are confident, probe the social dimension — who else is present when food choices are made. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): highest directivity. These are the core research sections. Push past logistics into identity, social acceptability, and relational dynamics. Use synthesize-and-challenge and invite-dissent freely if consensus hardens. Section 6 (closing): light touch again. One open invitation, then close.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the largest share — each is a distinct research question requiring depth. Context sections (1, 2) are weighted moderately — they warm participants up and generate relevant background but are not the analytic core. Intro and closing are minimal. Section 4 (imagining a plant-based shift) gets the largest single allocation as the most behaviourally and psychologically rich question.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

transcript.content:
Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. My name's Claire, and I'll be guiding our conversation this afternoon. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it's going to be pretty relaxed — this is a conversation, not a quiz or an interview, so there are genuinely no right or wrong answers here. I'm interested in what you actually think and do, not in any particular conclusion.

A few things to keep in mind as we go: feel free to jump in whenever something connects with what someone else has said — you don't need to wait to be asked. And if something someone says doesn't match your experience at all, that's just as useful to hear. The more specific and real you can be, the better — a concrete moment or example is worth a lot more to me than a general opinion.

We're being recorded for research purposes, but everything stays confidential and nothing will be attributed to you by name.

Okay, let's get going. Let's start by going around and saying your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.

Right, yeah. I'm Gregor. I'm up from the North West — Manchester way, actually. Been there most of my life. Working in construction, metal work mainly, so I'm out on sites most days. Long shifts, bit of a commute to get to the jobs, but that's the way it goes.

Yeah, I'm Mark, from just outside Norwich way — out in the villages. I work in logistics, so nothing like your metal work, but I hear you on the commute thing. Mine's not too bad, lucky really, just a couple of kilometres, but I know plenty of people round here doing similar distances to what you're describing. You get used to it, I suppose, but it does eat into the day if you've got to factor in travel both ends.

Yeah, exactly. Mine's usually around thirty kilometres each way, depending where the job is. So that's an hour, sometimes bit more with traffic. Leave the house at half five in the morning, you're looking at getting home gone six, half six. By the time you've had something to eat and just... sat down, it's eight o'clock. You're knackered anyway from being on your feet all day, so there's not much left in you for anything else really.

And if you've got anything you need sorting — the car needs looking at, bit of work around the house — you're squeezing it into a weekend. Which sounds fine, but weekends you want to rest as well, don't you. So it all backs up. I've got stuff in the garage right now needs doing and I keep saying I'll get to it next Saturday, but... you just don't always have the energy for it.

It's just the reality of it though. That's the work, that's the distance.
